claims.sentence: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec><jats:title>Background</jats:title><jats:p>Although “aspirin resistance” (AR‐inadequate platelet inhibition as suggested by in vitro testing of aspirin‐treated patients) has been widely studied in adults and linked to increased risk of adverse outcomes, its prevalence and clinical significance are largely unknown in children.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Procedure</jats:title><jats:p>To determine AR prevalence in children and its relationship to assay methodology, we undertook a cross‐sectional study of 44 children (1-17 years, 24 male) on aspirin for various indications and considered three published definitions of AR in adults: platelet aggregation ≥70% to 10 µM adenosine diphosphate and ≥20% to 0.5 mg/ml arachidonic acid (AA), normal PFA‐100® closure time and elevated urinary 11‐dehydro thromboxane B<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> (11dhTxB<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>) concentration.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Results</jats:title><jats:p>Six subjects exhibited AR according to at least one of the criteria (5 by PFA‐100®, 1 by aggregometry and 11dhTxB<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> criteria); nearly all subjects had low levels of 11dhTxB<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> compared with controls.
